title: The service desk with 61,000 messages
scenario:
You are the IT service manager at an insurance company with 3,000 staff. An AI assistant has answered staff IT questions for three months. It works next to the human service desk.

The CIO asks for a one-page view: "Is the assistant worth it?" The exhibit shows the vendor dashboard and a test the team ran on a cheaper model.
exhibit:
IT assistant: month 3 (made-up example data)

                               AI assistant        Human desk
Chats handled                  9,400               -
Messages generated             61,000              -
Tickets closed                 3,100               5,200
Resolution rate (same types)   55%                 88%
Median time to close           6 minutes           3.5 hours
Reopened within 7 days         14%                 5%
Thumbs-up rate                 91% (4% of users voted)

Model test: 500 past tickets, same prompt
                       Model M (current)    Model L (40% less per token)
Tickets resolved       410                  300
Total spend incl.      $30                  $27
retries

questions.prompt: Which numbers best answer the CIO's question?

options.text: Chats handled and messages generated, because they show how much the staff use it.
options.explanation: These are activity numbers. They show use, not whether problems were solved.

options.text: The 91% thumbs-up rate, because it comes straight from the staff who used the assistant.
options.explanation: Only 4% voted. Anthropic's post says user feedback is sparse and self-selected.

options.text: Tickets closed by the AI, because 3,100 tickets is a large number on its own.
options.explanation: A number alone has no baseline. It doesn't say how the AI compares with the human desk.

options.text: Resolution rate and time to close, AI vs human on the same ticket types, with reopens as a guard.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's accuracy guide compares human and AI on outcomes such as time to resolution. A guard number catches a hidden cost.

questions.prompt: The vendor's slide says: "91% of staff are happy." What is the best response?

options.text: Say the 91% comes from the 4% who voted; use it as one signal, not as everyone's view.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's post lists user feedback as sparse and self-selected. OpenAI's guide uses ratings next to other metrics.

options.text: Accept it: 91% is far above the 70% positive rating used in OpenAI's example.
options.explanation: OpenAI's example uses ratings as one metric among several. A 4% sample can't speak for all staff.

options.text: Drop feedback buttons completely, because user feedback is never useful.
options.explanation: Anthropic's post says feedback shows problems you didn't expect, with real examples. It is useful, just limited.

options.text: Ask the vendor to show the button to more staff until the rate reaches 95%.
options.explanation: The goal is an honest signal, not a higher number. A target for the rating invites gaming.

questions.prompt: Finance wants to switch to model L because it costs 40% less per token. What does the test show?

options.text: Switch: a 40% lower token price always means a lower total bill for the company.
options.explanation: The test shows the opposite. L needed retries and solved fewer tickets.

options.text: Keep M: it costs about $0.07 per resolved ticket against $0.09 for L, and it resolves more.
options.explanation: Right. $30 ÷ 410 ≈ $0.073 and $27 ÷ 300 = $0.09. Anthropic's cost guide says to compare cost per completed task, not per token.

options.text: Switch: L's total spend is $3 lower, so it is the cheaper option.
options.explanation: L is $3 cheaper in total but resolves 110 fewer tickets. Those tickets still go to people, at a much higher cost.

options.text: No decision is possible, because token prices change over time anyway.
options.explanation: Prices do change, but this test on your own tickets gives a clear answer today. Re-run it when prices change.

questions.prompt: AI tickets are reopened 14% of the time, human tickets 5%. How should the one-pager use this?

options.text: Leave it out, because the reopen rate is not a measure of quality.
options.explanation: A reopened ticket means the problem was not solved. That is a quality signal.

options.text: Leave it out, because the AI is still much faster at closing tickets than the human desk.
options.explanation: Speed doesn't help if many tickets come back. Hiding it makes the speed number look better than it is.

options.text: Show it as a guard number next to time to close, so speed is not read alone.
options.explanation: Right. A main KPI can improve while something else gets worse. OpenAI's guide shows how the cost of failures changes the decision.

options.text: Report only the human reopen rate, because the human desk is the baseline.
options.explanation: A baseline is for comparison. You need both rates to compare.
